lesson.title: Reading the Signs: The Compressibility Factor and When Gases Misbehave
lesson.summary: The compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT measures how far a real gas strays from ideal behavior, and the direction of that deviation reveals whether attraction or molecular volume dominates.
lesson.body:
Chemists have a simple diagnostic tool for measuring how real a gas is behaving: the compressibility factor, Z = PV/(nRT). For a perfectly ideal gas, Z is always exactly 1, by definition, since PV = nRT rearranges to give PV/nRT = 1. Any deviation of Z from 1 tells you, at a glance, which of the two Van der Waals corrections is winning under those particular conditions.

When Z is less than 1, the gas is more compressible than an ideal gas would be, meaning it takes up less volume, or exerts less pressure, than predicted. This happens when intermolecular attraction dominates: molecules are pulling each other inward, letting the gas squeeze into a smaller space more easily than a collection of non interacting particles would. This regime shows up at moderate pressures and lower temperatures, where molecules move slowly enough for attractive forces to have a real effect before the next collision.

When Z is greater than 1, the gas is less compressible than ideal, meaning it resists compression more than predicted. This happens at very high pressures, where molecules are packed so closely that their finite size, the excluded volume represented by b, becomes the dominant effect. No matter how hard you push, the molecules themselves take up real space and cannot be squeezed past a certain point. Gases with very weak attractions, like helium and hydrogen, tend to show Z greater than 1 across a wide range of pressures, because they have so little of an a term to pull Z below 1 in the first place.

Using the CO2 example from the last two chapters, we can compute Z directly. We found that 1.00 mol of CO2 in a 1.00 L container at 273 K has a Van der Waals corrected pressure of 19.82 atm, while nRT for that sample is 22.41 L atm. So Z = PV/(nRT) = (19.82 atm)(1.00 L)/(22.41 L atm) = 0.884. Since Z is well below 1, this confirms what we already suspected: under these compressed, low temperature conditions, CO2's intermolecular attractions dominate over its molecular volume, making the gas about 11.6 percent more compressible than ideal gas theory would predict. If we cooled this same sample further or compressed it more, Z would keep dropping, eventually heading toward the point where the gas condenses into a liquid entirely, a transition explored in the phase change chapters that follow.

It is worth remembering that Z is not a fixed property of a substance. The same gas can show Z less than 1 at one pressure and temperature and Z greater than 1 at another. Plotting Z against pressure at a fixed temperature typically produces a curve that dips below 1 at moderate pressure and then rises above 1 at very high pressure, tracing out the handoff from attraction dominated to volume dominated behavior.
